subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Representativeness: Judging by Resemblance
description: One-minute skill: Representativeness: Judging by Resemblance.

hook.text: Steve is shy and loves detail. Librarian or farmer? Most say librarian. But farmers outnumber librarians 20:1.

buildup.text: We judge probability by how well a description fits a category, ignoring the category's actual size.

discovery.text: Representativeness: we classify by similarity to a prototype, not by statistical likelihood.

twist.text: A sequence of HTHTHT looks less random than HHHHHH, yet both are equally probable in coin flips.

climax.text: Pattern-matching is fast and usually helpful. But when base rates matter, it leads us astray.

punchline.text: Looking the part isn't being the part.

quiz.question: What does the representativeness heuristic cause us to ignore?
options: How well a person fits a description

details.summary: The representativeness heuristic judges probability by how much something resembles a prototype. People estimate the likelihood that someone is a librarian based on how well they match the librarian stereotype, ignoring the base rate of librarians in the population.
details.whyItMatters: Representativeness leads to systematic probability errors by replacing statistical reasoning with pattern matching. It drives stereotyping, the conjunction fallacy, and neglect of base rates in domains from medical diagnosis to hiring decisions.
takeaways: People judge probability by resemblance to a category prototype
Base rate information is ignored when vivid case details are available
The conjunction fallacy occurs when a detailed description seems more likely than a general one

faq.question: What is the Linda problem and what does it demonstrate?
faq.answer: Linda is described as a philosophy major concerned with social justice. People rate 'Linda is a feminist bank teller' as more probable than 'Linda is a bank teller.' This violates logic because the subset feminist bank teller cannot be more probable than the broader category.

faq.question: How does representativeness affect hiring decisions?
faq.answer: Interviewers judge how well a candidate matches their mental image of the ideal employee rather than using base rates of success for similar candidates. This leads to hiring people who look the part over those who perform the part.
